cards.title: Agriculture's share of global emissions
cards.takeaway: Producing our food causes roughly a fifth to a third of all human greenhouse gas emissions, depending on what you count. Counting the whole food system, from farm and land clearing to processing, transport, retail and waste, it is about a third (32% in 2023).
cards.sayIt: "About a third of global emissions come from the food system. That's the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's own figure (FAO, 2025). Even if you only count farms and land clearing, it's over a fifth."

cards.title: Livestock's share of global emissions
cards.takeaway: Raising animals for meat, milk and eggs causes about 12% of all human greenhouse gas emissions (FAO, 2023). Animal-based foods produce more than half (57%) of food-production emissions (Xu et al., 2021) while supplying under a fifth (18%) of the world's calories (Poore & Nemecek, 2018).
cards.sayIt: "Livestock alone cause about 12% of global emissions. That's the latest estimate from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO, 2023). Animal foods are over half of food's climate footprint but give us less than a fifth of our calories."

cards.title: Agriculture's share of freshwater use
cards.takeaway: Farming is by far the largest user of fresh water. It takes about 70% of all freshwater withdrawn from rivers, lakes and aquifers (72% in FAO's latest data). Counting rainwater used by crops as well, agriculture makes up 92% of humanity's total water footprint (Hoekstra & Mekonnen, 2012).
cards.sayIt: "Around 70% of the fresh water we take from rivers and aquifers goes to farming. That's the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's figure (FAO, 2025). Industry and households share the rest."

cards.title: Animal products' share of agricultural water
cards.takeaway: Producing meat, dairy and eggs accounts for nearly a third of agriculture's total water footprint (Mekonnen & Hoekstra, 2012), and over half if all water on grazing land is counted (Weindl et al., 2017). Most of this is rainwater, mainly for feed and pasture. Counting only irrigation water, animal products' share is much smaller (roughly a sixth).
cards.sayIt: "Nearly a third of farming's water footprint goes to animal products (Mekonnen & Hoekstra, 2012). That's mostly rainwater on feed crops and pasture, so the bigger issue is how inefficiently animals turn that water into food."

cards.title: Water footprint of animal vs plant foods
cards.takeaway: For the same nutrition, animal foods need far more water than plant foods. Per calorie, beef's water footprint is about 20 times that of cereals and starchy roots. Per gram of protein, meat's footprint is 1.5 to 6 times that of pulses (beans, lentils, peas). The main reason is that animals turn only a small part of their feed into food (Mekonnen & Hoekstra, 2012).
cards.sayIt: "Calorie for calorie, beef takes about 20 times more water than grains or potatoes. Even for protein, meat needs up to six times more water than beans or lentils (Mekonnen & Hoekstra, 2012)."

questions.ask: Counting the whole food system (farming, land clearing, processing, transport, retail and waste), roughly what share of global greenhouse gas emissions does food cause?
questions.explain: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's 2025 brief puts agrifood systems at 16.5 Gt CO₂eq in 2023, 32% of global emissions. Crippa et al. (2021) independently found 34% for 2015.

questions.ask: Which boundary gives the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's (IPCC) figure of about 22% of global emissions?
questions.answer: AFOLU: agriculture, forestry & other land use
distractors: The whole food system, including supply chains
questions.explain: The IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report (Working Group III) found AFOLU produced 22% of global emissions in 2019. It covers farming plus land use (mainly deforestation), but not processing, transport or retail.

questions.ask: Counting only farm-gate emissions (crop and livestock production and on-farm energy), what share of global emissions is that?
questions.explain: Farm gate was 8.1 Gt CO₂eq of the food system's 16.5 Gt in 2023, which works out to ~16% of global emissions. 32% is the whole food system, not the farm gate.

questions.ask: Which component makes up the largest part of food-system emissions?
questions.explain: In 2023: farm gate 8.1 Gt (49%), supply chain 5.2 Gt (32%), land-use change 3.2 Gt (19%).

questions.ask: The food system's share of global emissions fell from 38% (2001) to 32% (2023). What happened to its actual emissions over that period?
questions.explain: The share fell only because other sectors grew faster. Food-system emissions rose 21% between 2001 and 2023.

questions.ask: According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) latest life-cycle estimate, what share of all human greenhouse gas emissions comes from livestock?
questions.explain: The FAO's 2023 Pathways report gives 6.2 Gt CO₂eq, about 12% of global emissions (reference year 2015). Avoid '51%': it comes from a non-peer-reviewed 2009 magazine article.

questions.ask: What was the UN Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) earlier, widely quoted 2013 estimate of livestock's share of global emissions?
questions.explain: Gerber et al. (FAO, 2013, reference year 2005) estimated 7.1 Gt CO₂eq, 14.5%. FAO's current figure is 12%. The methods changed, and the drop doesn't mean emissions fell.

questions.ask: What share of global food-production emissions comes from animal-based foods?
questions.explain: Xu et al. (Nature Food, 2021) found animal-based foods produce 57% of food-production emissions and plant-based foods 29%. Beef alone accounts for 25%.

questions.ask: Meat and dairy produce over half of food's emissions. What share of the world's calories do they provide?
questions.explain: Poore & Nemecek (Science, 2018): meat and dairy provide 18% of calories and 37% of protein, but use 83% of farmland.

questions.ask: Which animals account for the largest share of livestock emissions?
questions.explain: FAO (2023): cattle cause over 60% of livestock emissions, mostly from enteric methane. Pigs are ~15% and chickens ~9%.

questions.ask: Where does the often-repeated claim that livestock cause '51% of global emissions' come from?
questions.answer: A 2009 World Watch magazine article that was not peer-reviewed
distractors: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's (IPCC) Sixth Assessment Report
The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) 2023 Pathways report
A 2018 study in the journal Science
questions.explain: Goodland & Anhang (2009) published it in World Watch magazine, and the film Cowspiracy popularised it. It's widely criticised, so use FAO's 12% instead.

questions.ask: Roughly what share of the fresh water withdrawn from rivers, lakes and aquifers worldwide is used by agriculture?
questions.explain: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) 2025 AQUASTAT snapshot puts agriculture at 72% of freshwater withdrawals, industry at 15% and municipal use at 13%.

questions.ask: What share of global freshwater withdrawals goes to municipal use (homes and services)?
questions.explain: Municipal use is about 13% and industry 15%. Agriculture takes 72%, so diet matters far more for water than shower length.

questions.ask: Counting rainwater used by crops and the water needed to dilute pollution, what share of humanity's total water footprint comes from agriculture?
questions.explain: Hoekstra & Mekonnen (PNAS, 2012) found agriculture accounts for 92% of the global water footprint of 9,087 billion m³ a year (1996–2005).

questions.ask: In water-footprint accounting, what is 'green water'?
questions.answer: Rainwater stored in the soil and used by plants
distractors: Water taken from rivers and aquifers for irrigation
questions.explain: Green = rainwater in the soil. Blue = surface and groundwater (irrigation). Grey = the water needed to dilute pollution to safe levels.

questions.ask: Roughly what share of agriculture's total water footprint (rainwater, irrigation and pollution combined) goes to producing animal products?
questions.explain: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (Ecosystems, 2012) found 29% of agriculture's water footprint is for animal products. Counting all water on grazing land, Weindl et al. (2017) get 56%.

questions.ask: What kind of water makes up most of the water footprint of animal production?
questions.answer: Rainwater (green water) used by feed crops and pasture: ~87%
distractors: Irrigation water from rivers and aquifers
Water used in slaughterhouses and processing
questions.explain: Of 2,422 billion m³ a year, 87% is green (rain), 7% grey (pollution) and 6% blue (irrigation and drinking). Drinking water is a tiny part.

questions.ask: Counting all water used on grazing land, what share of agricultural water consumption is linked to livestock?
questions.explain: Weindl et al. (Global Environmental Change, 2017) estimate livestock-related water is 56% of agricultural water consumption, when all water on grazing land is counted.

questions.ask: Counting only irrigation (blue) water, roughly what share of agriculture's water footprint goes to animal products?
questions.explain: Calculated from Mekonnen & Hoekstra's figures: 151 of ~945 billion m³ of agricultural blue water. Most irrigation water goes to crops people eat directly, like rice and wheat.

questions.ask: Drinking and servicing water for farm animals is roughly what share of global freshwater use?
questions.explain: Drinking water is tiny (~0.6%, cited in Weindl et al., 2017). Livestock's water is almost all embedded in feed.

questions.ask: Per calorie, roughly how much larger is beef's water footprint than that of cereals and starchy roots?
questions.explain: Mekonnen & Hoekstra (Ecosystems, 2012): the average water footprint per calorie for beef is 20 times that of cereals and starchy roots.

questions.ask: Per gram of protein, how does meat's water footprint compare with that of pulses (beans, lentils, peas)?
questions.explain: Chicken is at the low end (~1.5×) and beef at the high end (~6×). Even for protein, plants need much less water.

questions.ask: What is the global average water footprint (green + blue + grey) of 1 kg of beef?
questions.explain: About 15,000 L/kg for beef, compared with ~6,000 for pork and ~4,300 for chicken. Most of it is rainwater on feed and pasture, so don't imply it all comes from taps or rivers.

questions.ask: Why do animal foods have larger water footprints than plant foods of the same nutritional value?
questions.answer: Animals convert only a small share of their feed into food, and the feed needs water to grow
distractors: Animals drink very large amounts of water
Slaughterhouses use most of the water
questions.explain: It's feed conversion. Drinking water is a tiny share (~0.6% of global freshwater use); the water is embedded in the feed.
